sets.title: A journey on the map
sets.summary: Students write imagined travel stories that use map directions, places and time-order transitions to sequence events.

tasks.prompt: Imagine you are visiting a town for the first time with a paper map. Write a story about how you found your way from the train station to the town museum.

fields: What I saw on the way

frames: I walked ___ (north, south, east or west) on ___.

models.text: I go train. I see map. I walk north. Big river. I see museum. Yay.
annotations: Tells events in order from start to finish.
Short sentences repeat the pattern I + verb.
Uses one direction word (north) and simple place words.

models.text: When I got off the train I opened my map. The museum was east of the station so I walked east on Main Street. On the way I passed a bakery and a big park with a fountain. Suddenly the street ended at a river and I was confuse. I look at the map again and I found a bridge. Finally I crossed the bridge and saw the museum.
annotations: Clear order with When, On the way, Suddenly and Finally.
Adds a problem (the river) and solves it.
Some past-tense errors (confuse, look) and missing commas after openers.
Uses map words: east, bridge, station.

models.text: As soon as I stepped off the train, I unfolded my map and found the museum, which was marked with a small star east of the station. I headed east along Harbor Road, passing a busy fish market and a hill covered in colorful houses. Then the road curved sharply, and I realized I was walking south instead! I checked the compass rose on the map, turned around, and crossed a stone bridge over the river. Ten minutes later, the museum's tall glass doors were right in front of me.
annotations: Events flow smoothly with time phrases (As soon as, Then, Ten minutes later).
Varied sentences, including a which clause and a series of actions.
Precise map words: compass rose, marked, headed east.
A small problem and its solution keep the reader interested.

checklist.text: My story goes in order from the station to the museum.
I started some sentences with time phrases like When I arrived or After that.
I used direction and map words like east, bridge and compass rose.

tasks.prompt: Imagine you are a child in a farming village long ago. Write a story about a day when your family took goods to trade at a market in a nearby town. Include what you hoped to trade, a problem, and how your family solved it.
frames: Long ago, in a small village, ___.
By the time we returned home, ___.

models.text: Long ago. I live farm. We take corn. Go to market. Man no want corn. We give eggs. He say ok. We go home happy.
annotations: Includes a setting, a problem and an ending.
Uses short phrases and simple sentences.
Drops some verb endings and small words (I live farm).

models.text: Long ago I lived in a small village with my family. We grew corn and beans on our farm. One morning before sunrise we packed our cart with corn and walked to the market in the next town. When we got there it was very crowded and noisy. We wanted to trade our corn for cloth. The problem was that the cloth seller already have a lot of corn. So my mother had a idea. She offered beans and corn together and the seller said yes. By the time we got home it was dark but we were happy with our new cloth.
annotations: Has a beginning, middle, problem, solution and ending.
Time phrases (One morning, When we got there, By the time) move the story forward.
Some errors (already have, a idea) and missing commas.
Uses trade words: trade, seller, offered.

models.text: Long ago, in a village surrounded by rice fields, my family woke before sunrise to prepare for market day. We loaded our wooden cart with sacks of rice and baskets of sweet potatoes, then walked three hours to the river town. The market was crowded with merchants calling out prices, and the smell of spices filled the air. We hoped to trade our rice for a new clay cooking pot, but the potter shook his head. He already had plenty of rice and needed salt instead. My father thought for a moment. Then he traded sweet potatoes to a salt merchant and offered the salt to the potter, who smiled and handed us the pot. By the time the stars came out, we were home, tired but proud of our clever plan.
annotations: Strong setting and a clear problem that is solved step by step.
Varied sentences: compound sentences, a who clause, and a short sentence for effect.
Sensory details (the smell of spices) and precise trade words (merchants, traded, offered).
The ending connects back to how the family felt.

checklist.text: My story has a setting, a problem, a solution and an ending.
I used time phrases to show when each part happened.
I wrote some longer sentences that join ideas with and, but, so or who.
I used trade words like merchant, goods and offered, and details the reader can see or smell.

sets.title: Where do puddles go?
sets.summary: Students explain the causes and effects of evaporation and condensation, using because, when, so and as a result.

tasks.prompt: After a rainstorm, there is a big puddle on the playground. By the afternoon, it is gone. Explain what happened to the water and why.

models.text: Puddle gone. Sun hot. Water go up air. Is evaporashun.
annotations: Names the cause (sun) and the effect (puddle gone).
Uses short phrases without connecting words.
Tries a science word using invented spelling.

models.text: The puddle disappeared because of the sun. When the sun shines on the puddle, the water get warm. The water turns into water vapor and goes in the air. You cant see it. As a result the puddle gets smaller and smaller and then it is gone. This is called evaporation.
annotations: Explains the cause and then the effect, in order.
Uses because, When and As a result to connect ideas.
Small errors (the water get, cant).
Uses science words: water vapor, evaporation.

models.text: The puddle did not vanish by magic; most of it evaporated. When sunlight warmed the puddle, tiny particles of water at the surface gained energy and escaped into the air as water vapor, an invisible gas. The breezy afternoon sped up the process because wind carries the vapor away. As a result, the puddle shrank little by little until the playground was dry.
annotations: Starts with a clear answer, then explains the steps of the process.
Complex sentences with When, because and until show cause and effect.
Precise science words: evaporated, particles, invisible gas.
Adds a second cause (wind) to make the explanation stronger.

checklist.text: I told the cause first and then the effect.
I used because, when or as a result to connect cause and effect.
I used science words like evaporation and water vapor.

tasks.prompt: On a hot day, you pour cold juice into a glass. Soon, tiny drops of water appear on the outside of the glass. Explain where the drops come from and why they form. Then explain how this is connected to the way clouds form.
frames: When warm air touches the cold glass, ___.
Clouds form in a similar way because ___.

models.text: Glass cold. Water on glass. Air have water. Cold make water. Clouds same.
annotations: Names the cold glass as a cause.
Uses short phrases; ideas are not yet connected.
Notices a link to clouds but does not explain it.

models.text: The water drops come from the air, not from inside the glass. The air has water vapor in it that we cant see. When the warm air touch the cold glass, the vapor gets cold and turns back into little drops of water. This is called condensation. Clouds are made the same way. Warm air go up in the sky where it is cold and the vapor turns into tiny drops. Then the drops make a cloud.
annotations: Explains the cause, the effect and the link to clouds in order.
Uses When to show cause and effect, but some ideas just follow each other.
Verb agreement errors (the air touch, warm air go).
Names the process: condensation.

models.text: Many people think the drops leak through the glass, but they actually come from the air around it. Air always holds some water vapor, an invisible gas. When warm, humid air touches the cold surface of the glass, it cools down quickly. Cool air cannot hold as much vapor, so some of the vapor changes back into liquid water. This change is called condensation, and it is the opposite of evaporation. Clouds form in a similar way. As warm air rises, it cools high in the sky, and its water vapor condenses onto tiny bits of dust. Millions of these droplets together make a cloud. Therefore, the wet glass and a cloud in the sky are examples of the same process.
annotations: Begins by correcting a common wrong idea, then explains step by step.
Cause-and-effect words (When, so, As, Therefore) link every step.
Precise words: humid, condenses, droplets, opposite of evaporation.
Clearly connects the small example (the glass) to the big idea (clouds).

checklist.text: I explained the glass first, then connected it to clouds, and ended with a conclusion.
I used sentences with when, so, as or therefore to show what causes what.
I used exact science words like condensation, water vapor and droplets.

sets.title: Choose our next class book
sets.summary: Students write opinion pieces about class reading choices, supporting a claim with reasons, examples and linking words, and answering another view.

tasks.prompt: Your class is choosing the next read-aloud book. Should the class read a graphic novel or a chapter book without pictures? Write your opinion and give two reasons.
frames: In my opinion, our class should read ___.

models.text: Graphic novel. Is fun. Picture help. I like.
annotations: States a choice.
Gives a reason in a short phrase (Picture help).
Uses simple, everyday words.

models.text: In my opinion our class should read a graphic novel. One reason is that the pictures help us understand the story. For example, if you dont know a word, you can look at the picture. Another reason is that more kids will want to listen because graphic novels are exciting. That is why I think we should read a graphic novel.
annotations: Gives an opinion, two reasons and a closing.
Linking words connect ideas: One reason, For example, Another reason, That is why.
Small errors (dont, a missing comma after In my opinion).

models.text: Our class should read a chapter book for our next read-aloud. First, a chapter book makes us picture the characters and places in our own minds, which builds our imagination. When our teacher read a mystery last spring, everyone imagined the old lighthouse differently, and we loved comparing our ideas. Second, chapter books include more descriptive language, so we learn new vocabulary. Although graphic novels are fun, a chapter book will help us grow as readers and listeners.
annotations: Clear opinion, two reasons with an example, and a strong closing.
Varied sentences, including When, which and Although clauses.
Precise words: imagination, descriptive language, vocabulary.
Mentions the other side (graphic novels are fun) before restating the opinion.

checklist.text: I stated my opinion, gave two reasons, and wrote a closing.
I used linking words like because, for example and another reason.
I used book words like characters, chapter and illustrations.

tasks.prompt: Some people think students should choose any book they want for independent reading. Others think teachers should choose the books. What do you think? Write an opinion piece with reasons and examples, respond to the other side, and end with a strong conclusion.

models.text: Kids pick book. Kids like. I like dog book. I read more. Teacher pick boring.
annotations: States an opinion.
Gives a personal example (dog book).
Short sentences; the word boring shows a feeling but not a reason.

models.text: I believe students should choose there own books. The first reason is that kids read more when they like the book. For instance, I read three books about soccer in one month because I love soccer. In addition, choosing books helps kids learn what they like. Some people think teachers should choose because they know good books but kids can ask the teacher for ideas. In conclusion students should choose there books.
annotations: Gives an opinion, two reasons, a response to the other side, and a conclusion.
Uses transitions: The first reason, For instance, In addition, In conclusion.
Spelling and punctuation errors (there own, missing commas).

models.text: I strongly believe students should be allowed to choose their own books for independent reading. The first reason is that choice makes reading more enjoyable, and students who enjoy reading usually read more often. For instance, my cousin used to avoid books until she discovered a series about young inventors; now she reads every night. In addition, choosing books teaches students to know themselves as readers, including which topics and authors they prefer. Some people argue that teachers should pick books because they know which ones are challenging enough. However, teachers can still guide students by suggesting a few options at the right level. In conclusion, when students choose, they become readers for life.
annotations: Organized with a clear opinion, two developed reasons, another view and a conclusion.
Long and short sentences, with clauses using who, because and when.
Precise words: independent, enjoyable, challenging, guide.
Answers the other side with However and a fair solution.

checklist.text: My opinion piece has reasons with examples, an answer to the other side, and a conclusion.
I used words like however, in addition and for instance to connect my ideas.
I wrote some sentences with who, because or when to add details.
I chose strong, exact words instead of words like good, bad or boring.
